newsitem.title: USA: U.S. money managers debt outlook steady-MCM Survey.
newsitem.headline: U.S. money managers debt outlook steady-MCM Survey.

text.p: U.S. money managers remained steady with their debt portfolios over the past week, keeping the 10-plus year duration sector at its highest level since last August, according to an MCM MoneyWatch Inc survey.

In the week ending July 28, 41 percent of investors polled overweighted the 10-plus years duration sector, up from 40 percent in the previous week. Seven percent underweighted it, while the remaining 52 percent were "neutral."
Significant shifts in asset class weightings were made over the past week, the report showed.

"The number being overinvested in governments rose sharply, while the comparable readings for corporates and mortgages fell equally, as they lagged Treasuries," said MCM MoneyWatch economist Astrid Adolfson, who conducts the weekly survey.
Cash as a percentage of assets dropped slightly to 3.24 percent from 3.25 percent registered the previous week.
Durations as a percentage of benchmark remained steady at 108.1 percent, the same throughout July.
A duration reading above 100 percent indicates the group of investors polled is mostly long on the market.
A portfolio's duration represents its average maturity and is used by portfolio managers to calculate exposure to risk.
In the "next likely move" category, portfolio managers representing 41 percent of total assets in the survey said they would "buy," higher than 38 percent in the prior week.
Strategists leaning toward "sell" dropped to 10 percent from 12 percent the previous week.
Forty-nine percent of managers said they were "neutral" on the market, down from 50 percent the prior week.
In the five- to 10-year duration sector, 40 percent of investors polled said they overweighted the securities and 22 percent underweighted them.
The survey included 38 domestic participants who manage about $110 billion in fixed-income assets. The poll is conducted weekly by MCM and usually is released on Tuesday.
